title: Κώνωψ καὶ λέων
part: The Gnat and the Lion (Chambry 188 · Perry 255)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 188 (= Perry 255). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κώνωψ πρὸς λέοντα ἐλθὼν εἶπεν· « Οὔτε φοβοῦμαί σε, οὔτε δυνατώτερός μου εἶ· εἰ δὲ μή, τί σοί ἐστιν ἡ δύναμις ; ὅτι ξύεις τοῖς ὄνυξι καὶ δάκνεις τοῖς ὀδοῦσι ; τοῦτο καὶ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρὶ μαχομένη ποιεῖ.
sentences.tr: Kōnōps pros leonta elthōn eipen· « Oute phoboumai se, oute dynatōteros mou ei· ei de mē, ti soi estin hē dynamis ; hoti xyeis tois onyxi kai dakneis tois odousi ; touto kai gynē tōi andri machomenē poiei.
sentences.l: A gnat, having come to a lion, said: « I neither fear you, nor are you more powerful than I; and if not, what is this power of yours? That you scratch with your claws and bite with your teeth? This a woman too does, fighting with her husband.
sentences.i: A gnat came to a lion and said: « I am not afraid of you, and you are no stronger than I am; or if you say otherwise, what does this power of yours amount to? That you scratch with your claws and bite with your teeth? A woman does as much when she is fighting her husband.
sentences.n: εἰ δὲ μή is a standing formula after a negative, "and if that is not so", picking up the denial just made. δυνατώτερός μου is the genitive of comparison, "stronger than I". The ὅτι clause is itself a question, put as the ground of the first: is that what your strength comes to? τοῖς ὄνυξι and τοῖς ὀδοῦσι are datives of instrument.

sentences.t: Ἐγὼ δὲ λίαν ὑπάρχω σου ἰσχυρότερος.
sentences.tr: Egō de lian hyparchō sou ischyroteros.
sentences.l: But I am far stronger than you.
sentences.n: ὑπάρχω does duty for εἰμί here, a use common in later Greek; σου is again the genitive of comparison.

sentences.t: Εἰ δὲ θέλεις, ἔλθωμεν καὶ εἰς πόλεμον. »
sentences.tr: Ei de theleis, elthōmen kai eis polemon. »
sentences.l: And if you wish, let us come even to war. »
sentences.n: ἔλθωμεν is the hortatory subjunctive, "let us…", the ordinary way Greek proposes a joint action.

sentences.t: Καὶ σαλπίσας ὁ κώνωψ ἐνεπήγετο, δάκνων τὰ περὶ τὰς ῥίνας αὐτοῦ ἄτριχα πρόσωπα.
sentences.tr: Kai salpisas ho kōnōps enepēgeto, daknōn ta peri tas rhinas autou atricha prosōpa.
sentences.l: And the gnat, having sounded the trumpet, drove himself in, biting the hairless faces around his nostrils.
sentences.i: And the gnat sounded his trumpet and fastened on, biting the bare skin about the lion's nostrils.
sentences.n: σαλπίζω is the war-trumpet, the signal that opens a battle; the gnat's whine is being read as a call to arms, and he sounds it again over the victory below. ἐνεπήγετο is the imperfect middle of ἐμπήγνυμι, to fix oneself into a thing. πρόσωπα is plural where English wants a singular — the several bare surfaces of the face.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ λέων τοῖς ἰδίοις ὄνυξι κατέλυεν ἑαυτόν, ἕως ἀπηύδησεν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho leōn tois idiois onyxi katelyen heauton, heōs apēudēsen.
sentences.l: And the lion with his own claws was undoing himself, until he gave out.
sentences.i: And the lion tore himself apart with his own claws until he could do no more.
sentences.n: καταλύω is to break up, to take to pieces what was put together — the lion dismantles himself. ἀπαυδάω is to give out, to be worn past bearing.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ κώνωψ νικήσας τὸν λέοντα, σαλπίσας καὶ ἐπινίκιον ᾄσας, ἔπτατο· καὶ ἀράχνης δεσμῷ ἐμπλακεὶς ἐσθιόμενος ἀπωδύρετο πῶς μεγίστοις πολεμῶν ὑπό εὐτελοῦς ζῴου, τῆς ἀράχνης, ἀπώλετο.
sentences.tr: Ho de kōnōps nikēsas ton leonta, salpisas kai epinikion āisas, eptato· kai arachnēs desmōi emplakeis esthiomenos apōdyreto pōs megistois polemōn hypo eutelous zōiou, tēs arachnēs, apōleto.
sentences.l: And the gnat, having conquered the lion, having sounded the trumpet and sung a victory-song, flew off; and, entangled in a spider's bond, being eaten, he lamented how, making war on the greatest, he was destroyed by a paltry creature, the spider.
sentences.i: And the gnat, having beaten the lion, sounded his trumpet, sang his victory song, and flew off; then, caught fast in a spider's web and eaten alive, he wailed that he who made war on the greatest should be destroyed by so cheap a creature as a spider.
sentences.n: ἐπινίκιον is the song sung over a victory, μέλος left unexpressed. πῶς after a verb of lamenting introduces an indirect exclamation — he bewails how it came about. πολεμῶν is concessive: though he warred with the greatest. Chambry prints ὑπό unelided before the vowel of εὐτελοῦς, and with the acute where running text would give the grave; the reading is left as printed.
